idiom_name: tokio::sync::Semaphore with acquire().await returning a drop-released permit
implementation_notes: Rust's standard library has no semaphore, and in async code the ecosystem realization is tokio::sync::Semaphore: acquire().await returns a SemaphorePermit that releases on drop - the RAII form of 'release on every exit path', including panics - acquire_many(n) takes several permits, try_acquire returns a TryAcquireError instead of blocking, acquire_owned moves a permit across task boundaries, and add_permits/forget_permits adjust the bound at runtime. Because the permit is a guard, the classic 'forgot to release' bug becomes an ownership question the compiler helps with, rather than a discipline problem.
pitfalls: mem::forget(permit) (or leaking the guard) loses the permit permanently - the same failure mode as a forgotten release, and the reason forget_permits exists explicitly.
The semaphore is fair (FIFO): a queued acquire_many at the head can block later single acquires even when enough permits are available for them, so weights must be planned together.
The Semaphore must outlive every waiter and every live permit; dropping it while permits are outstanding is legal but the bound no longer exists, which is easy to miss in long-lived tasks.

variants.name: std Mutex + Condvar hand-rolled semaphore
variants.idiom_name: std::sync::{Mutex, Condvar} with a permit counter
variants.implementation_notes: Synchronous Rust code has no semaphore in std, so the manual realization pairs a Mutex<usize> with a Condvar: acquire locks, waits with wait_while(|p| *p == 0) (the predicate form protects against spurious wakeups), then decrements; release increments and notify_one. It works on every Rust version with no runtime dependency, at the cost of writing and testing the waiter loop, and it must decide explicitly whether to use wait_timeout for a bounded wait. Use it when the callers are OS threads and pulling in an async runtime for a counter is not justified.
pitfalls: Mutex poisoning makes every unwrap() after a panicking holder a second failure; decide whether the permit counter may be poisoned and handle PoisonError deliberately.
notify_one after releasing the lock is usually preferable to notifying while holding it, but the counter must be updated under the same lock or a wakeup can be lost.
Condvar::wait can wake spuriously, so a bare if around it hands out permits that do not exist; always use the predicate (wait_while) form.
